title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E297 re-derives, by purely analytic means, the Euler equation of the isoperimetric/variational problem for ∫_0^a Z(x,y,p,q,r,s,…)dx, where p=y', q=y'', etc. It uses Lagrange's δ-algorithm, which Euler had adopted in E296 (Elementa calculi variationum) published the same year. Earlier pages wrote δZ=Nδy+Pδp+Qδq+…. With constant dx, δp=(δy)', δq=(δy)'', and so on. Repeated integration by parts (§21–22) then gives
δ∫Z dx = ∫ δy (N − P' + Q'' − R''' + S'''' − …) dx + δy(P − Q' + R'' − …) + (δy)'(Q − R' + …) + (δy)''(R − S' + …) + …,
with the 'absolute' (boundary) part evaluated at x=a.

This page (§22 end – §25):
(i) The higher-order formulas assume dx constant; δy is arbitrary at every x.
(ii) §23: for an extremum at x=a, the first variation must vanish for every choice of δy. In particular take a variation concentrated at a single interior value x<a. Then the final values of y at x=a are untouched, so δy=(δy)'=(δy)''=…=0 there and the absolute part vanishes. Only the integral part remains, and it must vanish.
(iii) §24: because the variation sits at a single point, the integral reduces to that one element. Hence N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − d³R/dx³ + d⁴S/dx⁴ − … = 0 at that point. Since the point is arbitrary, this holds for all x. This is the Euler(–Poisson) equation for higher-order Lagrangians, and it is independent of a.
(iv) §25: Euler notes it is the same equation as in his Methodus inveniendi (1744), now derived 'ex meris principiis analyticis'. The derivation succeeds because the reduction of §21 splits off boundary terms and leaves an integrand containing only ω=δy, without its derivatives.

On the following pages, the absolute terms yield the natural boundary conditions at x=a (P − Q' + R'' − … = 0, Q − R' + … = 0, …).

The argument is a heuristic version of the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations, using a 'point' variation.
errors: The boundary terms at the lower limit x=0 are silently ignored. The full absolute part is [δy(P − Q' + …) + (δy)'(Q − …) + …] evaluated from 0 to a. Euler treats it only at x=a (implicitly fixing the variation at x=0 or absorbing it into the integration constant). This does not affect the Euler equation but is a gap for the boundary conditions.

The 'variation at a single value of y' is not rigorous. A variation confined to one point contributes nothing to an integral, and its derivatives (δy)', (δy)'' would be singular. The correct form is a variation supported in a small neighbourhood with vanishing endpoint values (fundamental lemma; du Bois-Reymond, 1879). The conclusion is nevertheless correct for smooth integrands.

ideas.what: Derivation of the Euler–Poisson equation N − P' + Q'' − R''' + … = 0 via first variation and repeated integration by parts using Lagrange's δ-method
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi, 1744); analytic δ-derivation Lagrange (1755/1760–61), Euler E296/E297 (1766)
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi (E65), E296 Elementa calculi variationum, E297

ideas.what: Localized variation argument: vary y only at one interior point, so boundary terms vanish and the integrand must vanish pointwise
ideas.modern_name: Fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations (heuristic form)
ideas.where_published: E296, E297; also Lagrange's Miscellanea Taurinensia papers

ideas.what: Separation of the first variation into an integral part (containing only δy) and boundary ('absolute') parts, used later for endpoint conditions
ideas.modern_name: First variation formula with boundary terms; natural boundary conditions
ideas.where_published: E297 §§26–28; Lagrange, Essai d'une nouvelle méthode (1760–61)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the standard and well-documented Euler restatement of Lagrange's δ-derivation of the Euler equation. It is covered in histories of the calculus of variations (e.g., Goldstine, Fraser) and in the Opera omnia I.25 introduction. Nothing here is uncredited or unknown.
transcription_corrections: No substantive errors found; the transcription matches the image. Minor: 'inducuntur' (image) is grammatically 'inducitur' but is printed as transcribed.
